scenes.visual: Title card 'The Air Is a Tub' over a slowly rising and falling TEAL line. COLOUR MAP (both films): the air is a clear glass TUB labelled 'air' with a TEAL level marker and a ppm readout; GREEN arrows = photosynthesis (carbon out of the air); ORANGE arrows = respiration (in); BROWN arrows = decomposition (in); RED arrow = burning fossil fuels (in); DARK BLUE two-way arrow = ocean; LIGHT BLUE arrows and drops = water. Anchor organism: one big cartoon oak in a Virginia yard, with a deer and a rotting log. All drawings are cartoons labelled 'schematic'; any curve drawn from the 2025 Mauna Loa monthly values is labelled 'data: NOAA and Scripps, Mauna Loa'. Numbers appear only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: What pulls the carbon dioxide in the air down every summer, and what pushes it back up? Scientists on a Hawaiian volcano, Mauna Loa, have watched it happen every year since nineteen fifty-eight.
scenes.caption: What pulls the carbon dioxide in the air down every summer, and what pushes it back up? Scientists on a Hawaiian volcano, Mauna Loa, have watched it happen every year since 1958.
scenes.visual: A cartoon volcano in a blue ocean, a small station near its top labelled 'Mauna Loa, Hawaii'. A TEAL wavy line scrolls out of the station, dipping and rising; on-screen text 'measured since 1958'. A question card: 'down in summer... back up?'
scenes.narration: What pulls the carbon dioxide in the air down every summer, and what pushes it back up? Scientists on a Hawaiian volcano, Mauna Loa, have watched it happen every year since 1958.

scenes.tts: They count carbon dioxide in parts per million. Four hundred parts per million means four hundred carbon dioxide molecules in every million molecules of air. So it is only a tiny part of the air.
scenes.visual: A grid of one million tiny grey dots (drawn as a dense square) with 400 dots lit TEAL, labelled '400 ppm = 400 in every 1,000,000 molecules of air'. The lit dots pulse once.
scenes.narration: They count carbon dioxide in parts per million. Four hundred parts per million means four hundred carbon dioxide molecules in every million molecules of air. So it is only a tiny part of the air.

scenes.tts: Here is a way to think about it. Picture the air as a tub that holds carbon. A marker on the side shows the level, in parts per million.
scenes.visual: The dot grid pours into a clear glass TUB labelled 'air'. A TEAL level marker slides up its side with readout 'ppm'. The oak, a deer and a rotting log appear on the ground beside the tub.
scenes.narration: Here is a way to think about it. Picture the air as a tub that holds carbon. A marker on the side shows the level, in parts per million.

scenes.tts: One process drains the tub. Photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide out of the air. The oak in a Virginia yard builds that carbon into sugar.
scenes.visual: A GREEN arrow labelled 'photosynthesis' runs from the tub down into the oak's leaves; small sugar cubes appear in the leaves. The TEAL marker ticks down a little.
scenes.narration: One process drains the tub. Photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide out of the air. The oak in a Virginia yard builds that carbon into sugar.

scenes.tts: Other processes fill it. The oak and the deer both respire, day and night. Decomposers in the rotting log do too. Burning fuel adds more, and the ocean takes some in and gives some back.
scenes.visual: ORANGE arrows labelled 'respiration' rise from the oak and the deer (a small sun and moon icon cycle to show day and night). A BROWN arrow labelled 'decomposition' rises from the log, with fungi dots on it. A RED arrow labelled 'burning' rises from a smokestack. A DARK BLUE two-way arrow labelled 'ocean' links the tub to a strip of sea.
scenes.narration: Other processes fill it. The oak and the deer both respire, day and night. Decomposers in the rotting log do too. Burning fuel adds more, and the ocean takes some in and gives some back.

scenes.tts: Now the rule. The level goes up only when more flows in than flows out. It goes down only when more flows out than flows in.
scenes.visual: Big centred text builds: 'in > out: level rises' with the marker climbing; then 'out > in: level falls' with the marker dropping. Arrow widths change to match: thick orange beside thin green, then the reverse.
scenes.narration: Now the rule. The level goes up only when more flows in than flows out. It goes down only when more flows out than flows in.

scenes.tts: Watch one year. In spring the oak's leaves open, and photosynthesis speeds up. The oak still respires, and the log still rots. But out beats in, so the tub's level falls, month after month.
scenes.visual: Month strip along the bottom advances from April to August. Leaves burst onto the oak. The GREEN arrow thickens a lot; ORANGE and BROWN arrows thicken a little in the warmth but stay thinner than GREEN. A balance icon tips toward 'out'. The TEAL marker on the tub slides down. The tub is labelled 'model (schematic)'; no data line is drawn yet.
scenes.narration: Watch one year. In spring the oak's leaves open, and photosynthesis speeds up. The oak still respires, and the log still rots. But out beats in, so the tub's level falls, month after month.

scenes.tts: In fall, photosynthesis slows and the oak drops its leaves. Respiration and decomposition keep going. Now in beats out, so the level rises through fall, winter and spring.
scenes.visual: Month strip advances October to April. Leaves fall onto the log; the GREEN arrow thins to a thread. ORANGE and BROWN arrows thin a little in the cold but stay wider than GREEN. Balance tips toward 'in'. The tub's TEAL marker climbs (schematic model only; still no data line).
scenes.narration: In fall, photosynthesis slows and the oak drops its leaves. Respiration and decomposition keep going. Now in beats out, so the level rises through fall, winter and spring.

scenes.tts: Real air shows the same pattern. The line beside the tub is the record from Mauna Loa, for twenty twenty-five. The station measures the air itself, not each flow. The highest month is May. After that, the level falls all summer.
scenes.caption: Real air shows the same pattern. The line beside the tub is the record from Mauna Loa, for 2025. The station measures the air itself, not each flow. The highest month is May. After that, the level falls all summer.
scenes.visual: A separate framed graph panel appears beside the tub, with a thin divider between them: the tub keeps its label 'model (schematic)'; the panel is labelled 'data: NOAA and Scripps, Mauna Loa' and draws the full 2025 line with twelve monthly dots. Small note under the panel: 'measures the air, not each flow'. May's dot glows, label 'May 2025: 430.51 ppm'. A cursor slides down the summer months on the data panel only.
scenes.narration: Real air shows the same pattern. The line beside the tub is the record from Mauna Loa, for 2025. The station measures the air itself, not each flow. The highest month is May. After that, the level falls all summer.

scenes.tts: From July to August, the monthly average dropped the most. So is August the lowest month? Pause and decide.
scenes.visual: On the data panel, the July to August segment glows with label 'largest monthly drop: -2.39 ppm, July to August'. Question card: 'Is August the lowest month?'
scenes.narration: From July to August, the monthly average dropped the most. So is August the lowest month? Pause and decide.

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: No. The monthly average kept falling into September, the lowest month. In October it was higher again. A tub keeps draining as long as out beats in, so the bottom comes after the biggest drop.
scenes.visual: On the data panel, the cursor slides past August to September; September's dot glows, label 'September 2025: 424.37 ppm (lowest)'; October's dot sits a little higher. Separately, in the schematic tub, the marker slows, stops while the balance icon is level, then climbs as the balance tips to 'in'. Small text under the tub only: 'model: the level stops falling when out no longer beats in (schematic)'.
scenes.narration: No. The monthly average kept falling into September, the lowest month. In October it was higher again. A tub keeps draining as long as out beats in, so the bottom comes after the biggest drop.

scenes.tts: Now step back to many years. Burning coal, oil and gas adds old carbon from underground. Each year, a little more flows in than flows out.
scenes.visual: Zoom out: the tub sits on a timeline from 1958 to 2025. The RED burning arrow grows a little wider over the decades; a small coal seam under the ground is labelled 'old carbon'. The balance icon tips slightly toward 'in'.
scenes.narration: Now step back to many years. Burning coal, oil and gas adds old carbon from underground. Each year, a little more flows in than flows out.

scenes.tts: So the whole record climbs. To see the climb, compare the same month across the years, May with May. May against September only shows the yearly swing.
scenes.visual: Two dots light: 'May 1958: 317.51 ppm' and 'May 2025: 430.51 ppm', joined by a rising TEAL bracket labelled 'same month: the climb'. Then a short bracket between May 2025 and September 2025 labelled 'the yearly swing', drawn in grey. Schematic sketch, not the full record.
scenes.narration: So the whole record climbs. To see the climb, compare the same month across the years, May with May. May against September only shows the yearly swing.

scenes.tts: One tub, two patterns. The yearly swing comes from plants taking out more, then less, than is put back. The long climb comes mostly from burning.
scenes.visual: Split screen: left, the 2025 swing line labelled 'plants: out beats in, then in beats out'; right, the rising bracket labelled 'mostly burning: a little more in each year'. The tub sits in the middle.
scenes.narration: One tub, two patterns. The yearly swing comes from plants taking out more, then less, than is put back. The long climb comes mostly from burning.

scenes.visual: End card, one line only: 'The level moves only when in and out are unequal.'
